---
title: "Design principles"
---

*Written for version 0.1.6. Source: [`design-principles.md`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/figure-design/blob/main/plugin/skills/figure-to-interactive/references/design-principles.md).*

These are practical uses of established guidance, not rigid rules about appearance. The plugin uses them to find specific communication problems, never to strip out needed content or restyle a figure you've accepted.

## Composition before decoration

Choose an orientation and reading order that show the relationships. Steps in sequence line up; equivalent inputs get equal weight; exceptions sit beside the step they affect. Leave room for branching and merging arrows before placing boxes. Avoid unnecessary crossings, bends and reversals. Use clear junctions and arrowheads; two things being close together must not be the only sign that they're related.

Background: yWorks on [layered graph layout](https://www.yworks.com/pages/layered-graph-layout.html) and [orthogonal edge routing](https://yed.yworks.com/support/manual/layout/router_orthogonal.html). These describe the ideas; the plugin doesn't need their software, and automatic layouts still have to be inspected.

## Connectors and arrows

Version 0.1.6 turns the principles above into numbered rules, so a check or a reviewer can cite the rule a figure breaks. The assistant applies them when drawing, and again after any revision that moves a box or a line. Rules marked *code* can be checked by a script on the rendered SVG; rules marked *look* need judgment. The distances are the plugin's defaults and can change for a particular figure.

| Rule | What it says | Check |
|----|-------------------------------------|------|
| A1 | Each arrow shows one real relationship and points the way the thing moves. | look |
| A2 | If an arrow's meaning isn't obvious from its ends, label it on the arrow, not in a legend. | look |
| A3 | Remove crossings by moving boxes before rerouting lines; aim for none. | code |
| A4 | An unavoidable crossing is at a right angle, away from labels and arrowheads, with a gap or contrasting colours, so it can't be read as a junction. | code and look |
| A5 | A line never passes through a box, icon or text it doesn't connect to, and keeps 8 px from them. | code |
| A6 | Parallel lines stay 8 px apart and never share a path unless they deliberately merge. | code |
| A7 | Straight or right-angled lines, with at most two bends (three along an outer channel). | code |
| A8 | Arrows meet a box at the middle of a side, on the side facing the flow. | code |
| A9 | Arrowheads touch the target's edge, and lines start at the source's edge. | code |
| A10 | Branches and merges use one trunk and a visible junction dot; a plain crossing never has a dot. | code and look |
| A11 | The main flow runs one way; return arrows go around the outside. | look |
| A12 | Two-way arrows only for genuinely two-way relationships. | look |
| A13 | Each line style has one meaning, explained once in a key. | code |
| A14 | Long routes run along open channels, or use labelled connectors such as "to 6". | look |

## Layout, alignment and labels

| Rule | What it says | Check |
|----|-------------------------------------|------|
| L1 | Boxes in a row or column line up, within 2 px. | code |
| L2 | Equal gaps between stages; bigger gaps between groups than within them. | code |
| L3 | Boxes are sized to their text at final size; text is never shrunk to fit. | code |
| L4 | Nothing within 12 px of the edge, and nothing clipped. | code |
| L5 | No crowded region beside a large empty one. | look |
| L6 | Reading order follows the flow; stages are numbered when order matters. | look |
| T1 | Labels are horizontal. | code |
| T2 | No line runs through text. | code |
| T3 | Each label sits closest to what it names. | code |
| T4 | Text meets the destination's minimum size: 8 pt in print, about 11 px on screen. | code |

These rules are the plugin's own synthesis, not a published standard. They restate the principles on this page and the [lessons from earlier figures](style.qmd#lessons-from-earlier-figures), add common diagramming conventions, and were adjusted after checking them against the TransplantID reference, which uses contrasting colours at crossings and long routes along open channels. Bang Wong's *Points of View* columns in *Nature Methods*, such as ["Arrows"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1676) and ["Layout"](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1711) (both 2011), are related reading that hasn't yet been checked against these rules.

## Hierarchy and grouping

Make the main explanation dominate through size, position, contrast and white space. Group related elements by placing them close together or inside a shared region. Keep alignment and spacing consistent. Important distinctions shouldn't rely on colour alone. Setup steps and footnotes shouldn't look as important as the central action.

Background: Nielsen Norman Group on [principles of visual design](https://media.nngroup.com/media/articles/attachments/Principles_Visual_Design-A4.pdf), [proximity](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/gestalt-proximity/) and [visual hierarchy](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/visual-hierarchy-ux-definition/).

## Text, illustrations and shared objects

Use a restrained set of type sizes, readable line lengths and clear space around labels. Measure the rendered text and make the container fit it, rather than shrinking the text until it fits. The same object has the same role, colour and illustration in every view. Illustrations other than logos form one family; logos are authentic and their source is kept. Decoration must not change what the figure says.

## Audience and medium

Choose the content and the way it's drawn for the reader and where they'll see it. The overview has to work before anything is clicked. A large figure scaled down can be technically complete and still unreadable, so inspect it at the size it will be seen, and plan enlarged viewing or section crops when needed.

Background: Rougier, Droettboom and Bourne, ["Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures"](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833) (*PLOS Computational Biology*, 2014). That paper is general advice for scientific figures, not a standard for workflow diagrams; the plugin's checks are its own summary rather than rules quoted from any one source.
